title: French heritage and French songs in Louisiana
summary: He is entirely French, fifth or sixth generation; his mother sang French songs, and he explains three French dialects in Louisiana.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well that's funny. A lot of you fellas seem to have studied under the Italians. But you're not an Italian at all. No, I'm French. Entirely French, huh?
Yeah, both sides of them. In fact, let me see, I'm the fifth or sixth generation in this country, in Louisiana.
Let's see, now I wanted to ask you about some of those French songs. Did you ever hear any French songs when you were young?
Oh yeah, my mother used to sing quite a few of them. I think I just about forgot most of them, you know, little ditties and French folk songs, you know.
I wondered if they picked any of them up in the jazz occasionally.
I think they have. I've heard some of them recorded already.
Well that A-Law-Bah, they have several recorded songs.

That was a colored song. Because, you see, there were more or less three different French dialects in Louisiana. The Negro dialect and what they call a Cajun, and then the true French. My mother and father were both educated in Louisiana but in French. And at home conversations were all held in French. My mother would speak French to us and we'd answer in English. So then it finally came to a point that she'd speak half a sentence in French and half of a sentence in English, you know.
